deep.reconstruction:
Context. This page is the draft of the proof of 'Lehrsatz 3' in §8 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published by Dedekind in 1867). In that paper the series is Ω = A_0 + Σ A_n with A_n = a_n sin nx + b_n cos nx and A_n → 0 for every x. F is the twice formally integrated series: F(x) = C' + C''x + A_0 x²/2 − Σ_{n≥1} A_n/n². Lehrsatz 3 says: if b<c, and λ and λ' are continuous on [b,c] and vanish at b and c, and λ'' has only finitely many maxima and minima, then μ² ∫_b^c F(x) cos μ(x−a) λ(x) dx → 0 as μ → ∞. This is Riemann's localization principle.

Step 1. Substitute the series for F, integrating termwise (justified because Σ A_n/n² converges uniformly). This gives the series (Φ):
μ² ∫_b^c (C' + C''x + A_0 x²/2) cos μ(x−a) λ dx − Σ_{n=1}^∞ (μ²/n²) ∫_b^c A_n cos μ(x−a) λ dx.

Step 2. By the product-to-sum formulas, A_n cos μ(x−a) is a linear combination of cos(μ+n)(x−a), sin(μ+n)(x−a), cos(μ−n)(x−a) and sin(μ−n)(x−a). Call the first pair's sum B_{μ+n} and the second pair's sum B_{μ−n}. Then:
- A_n cos μ(x−a) = B_{μ+n} + B_{μ−n};
- B''_{μ±n} = −(μ±n)² B_{μ±n};
- the coefficients are (a_n, b_n)/2 rotated by the angle na, so B_{μ±n} → 0 as n → ∞, uniformly in x.

Step 3. The general term of Φ becomes
−(μ²/n²) ∫ A_n cos μ(x−a) λ dx = μ²/(n²(μ+n)²) ∫ B''_{μ+n} λ dx + μ²/(n²(μ−n)²) ∫ B''_{μ−n} λ dx.
Integrating by parts twice, with boundary terms vanishing because λ(b)=λ(c)=λ'(b)=λ'(c)=0, this equals
μ²/(n²(μ+n)²) ∫_b^c B_{μ+n} λ'' dx + μ²/(n²(μ−n)²) ∫_b^c B_{μ−n} λ'' dx.

Step 4. sup_n |∫_b^c B_{μ±n} λ'' dx| → 0 as μ → ∞. Either μ±n is large, and then ∫ cos/sin((μ±n)(x−a)) λ'' dx → 0 (Riemann–Lebesgue for λ''). Or μ±n stays bounded, and then n must be large, so the coefficients of B are small.

Step 5 (reduction). Let n run over all integers, so the μ+n terms are absorbed as μ−(−n). Then it suffices to show that
S(μ) = Σ μ²/((μ−n)² n²), taken over n < −c', c'' < n < μ−c''', n > μ+c^{IV},
stays bounded as μ → ∞. The excluded terms (−c'<n<c'' and μ−c'''<n<μ+c^{IV}) are finitely many and individually tend to 0. The rest of Φ is at most S(μ) · max|∫ B_{μ±n} λ''|, which tends to 0.

Step 6. Write μ²/((μ−n)² n²) = (1/μ) · (1/μ)/((1−n/μ)² (n/μ)²). For constants c > 1 the sum is less than (1/μ) ∫ dx/((1−x)² x²) over the corresponding x-ranges. This is a Riemann-sum comparison using the monotonicity of the integrand on each range, completed on the next page with the explicit antiderivative −1/x + 1/(1−x) + 2 log x − 2 log(1−x). Near the endpoints x ~ c/μ the integral is O(μ), so S(μ) = O(1).

Omitted step (mine). The polynomial term μ² ∫ (C' + C''x + A_0 x²/2) cos μ(x−a) λ dx → 0 must also be handled. It does: integrate by parts twice and apply Riemann–Lebesgue to ((C' + C''x + A_0 x²/2) λ)''. The draft does not address this term on this page.
errors: The polynomial (first) term of Φ is not treated on this page. It tends to 0 by the same double integration by parts, but the step is omitted.

For the finitely many excluded terms with n near μ, the coefficient μ²/(n²(μ−n)²) can blow up, e.g. when μ is an integer and n = μ. These terms must be estimated directly from −(μ²/n²) ∫ A_n cos μ(x−a) λ dx, where μ²/n² is bounded and A_n → 0. The text just says 'offenbar unendlich klein'. This is correct but tacit.

The bound on Φ tacitly treats the μ+n terms by letting n range over negative integers, so the coefficient μ²/(n²(μ+n)²) becomes μ²/(n²(μ−n)²) with n → −n. This explains the condition n < −c', but the reindexing is not stated.

Notation is inconsistent with the continuation. The lower bound of the middle range is c'' here, but the next page writes (c'+1)/μ. The next page also writes −(c'''−1)/μ where 1 − (c'''−1)/μ is meant.
Step 4 needs uniformity in n of the Riemann–Lebesgue decay, i.e. sup over n of |∫ B_{μ±n} λ''| → 0. The two-case argument sketches this adequately, given that λ'' is integrable (piecewise monotone).

results.what: μ² ∫ F(x) cos μ(x−a) λ(x) dx → 0 for the twice-integrated series F of a trigonometric series with coefficients tending to 0, for smooth cutoffs λ vanishing to first order at the endpoints
results.modern_name: Riemann's localization principle (Riemann's third lemma / Riemann's second lemma in some texts) for trigonometric series

results.what: Termwise product-to-sum decomposition plus double integration by parts, converting μ²/n² ∫ B'' λ into μ²/(n²(μ±n)²) ∫ B λ''
results.modern_name: integration by parts / Riemann–Lebesgue lemma technique

results.what: Bound of Σ μ²/((μ−n)² n²) over n away from 0 and μ by (1/μ) ∫ dx/(x²(1−x)²), giving O(1)
results.modern_name: integral comparison of a Riemann sum

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the proof of Lehrsatz 3 (the localization principle) from Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series. It matches the printed text nearly verbatim and is well known as his.

checkable.asserts: trivial sanity; see next item for the product-to-sum split
cos μ(x−a)·cos nx splits into a (μ+n)-frequency part and a (μ−n)-frequency part in the variable x−a (defining B_{μ+n}, B_{μ−n})
antiderivative of 1/(x²(1−x)²) used on the next page (result 0)
numerical spot check that the middle-range sum stays bounded (≈ 2·ζ(2)+... finite) for large μ

transcription_corrections: The first summation condition should read 'n < −c′' (n < −c'), not 'n > c′'. The excluded range '−c′ < n < c″' and the published text confirm this.
In the series Φ the integrand is cos μ(x−a); a struck-through character precedes 'cos' in the manuscript, but the intended function is cos.

The margin note is a revised wording of the sentence about the integrals ∫ cos/sin(μ±n)(x−a) λ''(x) dx. It reads roughly '... die Integrale, und wenn μ±n unendl. gross wird, so werden diese Integrale, wenn aber nicht, weil dann in diesem Falle n unendl. gross wird, ihre Coefficienten unendlich klein.' Its first words are uncertain.
